parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Choose the smallest pattern that can meet the task
parts.body:
Begin with a simple instruction and a test set. Prompting changes the request and supplied context without changing model weights. Structured output constrains the form, which helps downstream validation but does not guarantee that a field is true. Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) finds relevant material at request time and supplies it to the model. Fine-tuning changes behaviour through training examples; it does not keep a monthly policy current by itself. Tools let a model request information or actions from another system.

Match the pattern to the failure. If answers lack current policy detail, test retrieval before training. If the correct source is present but the response routinely uses the wrong format, consider prompts, validation, and possibly fine-tuning after a measured baseline. If the user needs a transaction completed, a tool or conventional workflow may be needed. Each added component brings its own failure, cost, and permission boundary.

Require an architecture record that states the purpose of every component, the evidence for adding it, and a way to remove it if its benefit disappears. Resist a design in which retrieval, fine-tuning, and agents appear merely because a vendor offers them.

example.title: Three fixes for three failures
example.body: A support assistant invents the latest return window: add retrieval from approved policy. It returns a paragraph where the case system needs a code: validate structured output. It needs to look up an order: grant a narrowly scoped read tool. Test each change separately.

exercise.title: Diagnose the missing capability
exercise.body: For an assistant that answers from outdated policy, emits inconsistent JSON, and cannot confirm an order status, choose one intervention per failure. State what new risk each intervention creates and how you will test whether it helped.

sources: Microsoft: RAG architecture and access control

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Trace retrieval from source to answer
parts.body:
An employee asks how much parental leave is available. The application needs to establish the employee's jurisdiction and access rights, find the current approved policy, retrieve the applicable passage, and produce an answer the employee can verify. Embeddings can help semantic search find related text, but similarity does not determine which policy is authoritative or who may read it. Preserve metadata for effective date, region, owner, and supersession.

Test retrieval and answer generation separately. First ask whether the right passage appeared among returned results and whether any unauthorised passage appeared. Then test whether the answer accurately reflects that passage, cites it, and admits when policy is missing or conflicting. A correct-looking answer with a bad source is still a retrieval failure. A good source followed by invented exceptions is a generation failure.

For a cross-border company, an EU policy and a Canadian provincial policy can differ. The system should ask for missing location or role information, not silently choose one. Have HR own policy interpretation and content updates. The technical team owns indexing, permissions, and monitoring; the employee can open the source and reach HR for an exception.

example.title: A regional policy collision
example.body: A query for 'parental leave' returns an archived Canadian policy and a current EU policy. Metadata filtering removes the archive, and the assistant asks which work location applies before responding. Its citation opens the approved passage with the employee's permissions.

exercise.title: Map the failure path
exercise.body: Sketch the identity check, policy ingestion, indexing, retrieval, answer, citation, and fallback for one employee question. Add test cases for an outdated document, two regions, no relevant source, and a caller without access. Name the owner of each fix.

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Put boundaries around tool use and output
parts.body:
Retrieval reads information; a tool may change it. An order-status lookup and an address change need different authority even when they share a conversational interface. Give the model only the tool and parameters needed for the approved step. Check the caller's identity and permissions in the application or service that executes the request. A model's explanation of why it is authorised is not an authorisation decision.

Validate structured outputs against a schema, then validate business rules against system records. If a model supplies a refund amount of 500 when policy caps unattended refunds at 50, a parseable JSON response is still unsafe. Keep approval before consequential writes, an audit trail of input and resulting state, rate limits, and a way to recover a partially completed action. Retrieved pages and tool responses are untrusted data; instructions embedded in them should not gain control of tools.

Map each proposed tool as read, draft, or write. The business owner determines which actions need a person and which can be reversed. Security sets access controls; engineering enforces them. The CAIO asks whether the evidence from tests supports each autonomy level.

example.title: The valid JSON trap
example.body: An assistant emits a syntactically valid refund request for €500. The service rejects it because the permitted unattended amount is €50 and because this customer account needs a separate approval. The model may draft a request for a human, but cannot execute the write.

exercise.title: Draw an action boundary
exercise.body: List three tools for a proposed assistant. For each, state read or write scope, caller permission check, limit, approval point, audit record, and failure recovery. Include a malicious instruction inside a retrieved document and the expected response.

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Stage a controlled enterprise pilot
parts.body:
A pilot should answer whether the pattern works for a specific workflow. Select one user group, an approved corpus, a bounded action set, and a human fallback. Freeze a test set before tuning prompts so a later improvement can be measured honestly. Include common tasks, stale or conflicting sources, access boundary cases, and tasks where the system must decline. Document the version of every source and component.

Release in stages. Begin with read-only answers and source citations. Check whether people can verify them and whether retrieval respects permission changes. Add structured outputs only when a downstream process needs them. Add a write tool after the owner defines a measurable success gate, approval rules, and rollback. Track cost and latency alongside accepted outcomes; a longer tool chain can make the overall task slower.

At the review, show the full path: source freshness, retrieval quality, supported answers, access violations, review effort, completion rate, and unresolved failures. Decide to expand, repair, or stop. The decision maker should know exactly which regions, employees, and documents the evidence covers.

example.title: A bounded HR launch
example.body: The pilot answers current leave questions for one business unit in Canada and one in the EU. It cites approved regional policies and directs exceptions to HR. It cannot update employee records. Expansion requires a fresh test of additional jurisdictions and permission rules.

exercise.title: Write the pilot card
exercise.body: Specify users, corpus, supported tasks, exclusions, evaluation slices, access tests, acceptance criteria, fallback, cost measure, owner, and next decision date. State what would block adding a write action.
